questions.q: Why does this lesson say every defense built earlier in the course (injection prevention, red-teaming, monitoring, bias testing) still doesn't guarantee incidents never happen?
options: Because those defenses are completely ineffective and provide no benefit at all
Because each control reduces the odds and shortens time-to-detection of a failure, but none of them makes failure impossible
Because incident response is only needed for systems with no defenses at all
Because defenses only apply during development, never in production
questions.explain: The lesson frames every earlier control as a risk reduction, not an absolute guarantee, which is why a response plan is still needed for the day something gets through.

questions.q: What is the AI-specific wrinkle in the 'Contain' stage of incident response, according to this lesson?
options: Containment for AI incidents is always identical to reverting a single line of code, just like traditional software bugs
Unlike a traditional bug, there's often no single line of code to revert — containment might mean rolling back a model version, tightening a prompt, or disabling the feature
AI systems can never be contained once an incident starts
Containment only applies to incidents that involve a security breach
questions.explain: The lesson highlights that AI incidents often lack a clean code-level fix, requiring different containment actions like model rollback or prompt changes.

questions.q: How does this lesson say a harmful hallucination incident should be contained, beyond just fixing the one instance?
options: By deleting all records of the incident so it cannot be referenced again
By adding the failure case to the eval dataset immediately, not just fixing that one instance
By disabling the entire AI system permanently with no further action
By ignoring it unless the exact same hallucination happens a second time
questions.explain: The lesson specifies that containing a hallucination incident means feeding it into the eval dataset so similar cases get caught going forward, not just patching the one occurrence.

questions.q: What does this lesson say a postmortem's real output should be?
options: A list of which team members are personally to blame for the incident
An honest answer to which earlier control (eval, drift check, alert, bias test) should have caught the incident, and why it didn't
A press release announcing the incident is fully resolved
A decision to stop using any form of monitoring going forward
questions.explain: The lesson frames the postmortem's purpose as identifying which existing control should have caught the issue, not assigning blame.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an incident that doesn't change the eval dataset, alert thresholds, or documentation 'was reviewed, not actually learned from'?
options: Because closing the loop — feeding the incident's lesson back into evals, alerts, or docs — is what prevents the same failure from recurring; without that, nothing in the system actually improves
Because every incident must always result in firing someone
Because postmortems are purely ceremonial and have no real effect under any circumstances
Because only security incidents, never bias or hallucination incidents, require follow-up changes
questions.explain: The lesson's central point is that real learning from an incident shows up as a concrete change to an eval, an alert threshold, or documentation — not just a discussion.
